laibi.title: Superette Laibi
laibi.summary: I built a supermarket website for people in Bouira to order groceries from home. The owner uses the same system to update the store and manage every order.
laibi.contribution: I planned the product, designed the customer and admin screens, built the full system, and put it online.
laibi.result: One small ad campaign brought about 50% ROI in the first 27 days. 94.4% of orders were delivered.

images.cardAlt: Supermarket Laibi 2 web app project card

context.title: The supermarket only sold to people who came in
context.body: The owner wanted online orders without spending hours updating a second system. Stock, prices, photos, and orders had to stay simple.

build.title: I built the store and the tools behind it
build.body: Customers browse, search, filter, add to cart, and order. The owner manages products, stock, images, and orders, with Excel imports and instant alerts. We used a PWA for the website and installable phone app. It runs on an Oracle VPS behind Cloudflare.

outcome.title: One small campaign brought real orders
outcome.body: The platform reached about 50% ROI in its first 27 days. The owner ran one small ad campaign, and 94.4% of orders were delivered.

said.title: Said
said.summary: I built an online catalog for a heavy-truck-parts seller in Algiers. Buyers search by part number, brand, truck model, and stock before they call or order.
said.contribution: I planned the catalog, designed the mobile flow, built the search and order pages, and made the working prototype.
said.result: The goal is to reach buyers across Algeria and spend less time sending photos or answering stock questions. The store still uses test data.

images.cardAlt: Said heavy truck parts store project preview
images.mobileAlt: Said mobile shopping experience for heavy truck parts

context.title: Buyers kept asking the same questions
context.body: Do you have this part? What is the number? Does it fit my truck? Is it in stock? The seller had to answer each person by hand.

build.title: I made the stock easy to search
build.body: I built search, categories, brand pages, part details, saved items, a cart, order tracking, and admin tools. We placed the part number and fit details first.

outcome.title: Ready for the seller’s real stock
outcome.body: The prototype is ready for real product data. It has not been used for live sales, so I do not show sales results.

rimoochat.title: Rimoochat
rimoochat.summary: I built Rimoochat to sell handmade dresses and home textiles online. Customers see the full range, check each item, and order without digging through old posts or messages.
rimoochat.contribution: I planned the store, designed the pages, built the frontend, and made the mobile order flow.
rimoochat.result: The store has helped increase sales over the last few months. It also gives customers one clear place to browse and order.

context.title: Selling through messages made each order harder
context.body: Customers had to ask what was available, wait for photos, and repeat the same questions. Busy social feeds also made handmade pieces look like common products.

build.title: I gave every product its own page
build.body: I built a simple store with clear photos, prices, product details, and a short order flow. We kept the design soft so the handmade work stays in focus.

outcome.title: More sales in recent months
outcome.body: Rimoochat is now in use. It has helped the business sell more while giving customers a simpler way to browse and order.

unimarket.title: Unimarket
unimarket.summary: I built Unimarket to put social shopping and online stores in one app. People follow sellers, see new products, save items, and place orders.
unimarket.contribution: I planned the product, designed the seller and buyer flows, and built the full platform.
unimarket.result: The main product is ready and Unimarket is now in its launch stage. Sales and user results will come after the launch.

context.title: A product post disappears fast
context.body: Sellers keep posting and paying to reach buyers. Old products move down the feed, and orders end up mixed with normal messages.

build.title: I joined the feed and the store
build.body: Sellers get store pages, products, followers, and order tools. Buyers follow, like, save, share, and order. We planned live sales and bidding, but did not ship them.

outcome.title: Unimarket is getting ready to launch
outcome.body: The main seller and buyer flows are ready. The current work is focused on launch, so there are no public sales or user numbers yet.

roadmap.title: Auctions, product reels, and delivery connections
roadmap.body: Live auctions, short product videos, and delivery-agency integrations are on the roadmap. They are planned features, not shipped claims.

duks.title: DUKS Perfume
duks.summary: I made a fun Arabic-first website for DUKS Perfume. It uses bold photos, type, layout, and motion to give the perfume its own visual world.
duks.contribution: I made the idea, visual style, Arabic pages, mobile layout, and frontend.
duks.result: DUKS liked the prototype a lot, but he could not use it because of his contract with Ayor.

images.cardAlt: DUKS perfume experimental website project card
images.mobileAlt: Arabic-first DUKS perfume experience on mobile

context.title: A perfume page should feel like the product
context.body: I wanted to see how far one perfume could carry a full website when the page had its own look, pace, and story.

build.title: I built the whole page around one perfume
build.body: I used strong photos, Arabic type, motion, and a short product story. We kept the page focused and gave desktop and mobile their own layout.

outcome.title: A fun design and frontend project
outcome.body: I kept the finished prototype as a visual and frontend experiment.

reperto.contribution: I plan the product structure, make the technical choices, build the system, and lead delivery.
reperto.result: There is no public link. I will share the full project after the client approves it.

context.title: The project stays private for now
context.body: The client has not approved a public case study. I keep the product, screens, and business details private.

build.title: I lead the technical work

outcome.title: Waiting for approval to share

tahwisa.title: Tahwisa
tahwisa.summary: I built Tahwisa for a travel agency. The team uses it every day to track clients, bookings, payments, debts, expenses, and the money held by each worker.
tahwisa.contribution: I planned the system, built the money and booking flows, developed the full app, and made it installable.
tahwisa.result: The agency now checks unpaid balances, due dates, client requests, costs, profit, and staff cash transfers in one place.

context.title: The agency was losing track of money and tasks
context.body: Clients pay in parts. Workers pass money between each other. Bookings, due dates, costs, and client requests were spread across messages and memory.

build.title: I gave every payment a clear record
build.body: Each payment shows the client, service, amount, and worker who received it. We also track debt, due dates, costs, profit, requests, and cash transfers.

outcome.title: The agency now uses it every day
outcome.body: The owner sees what clients owe, what each worker holds, what the agency spent, and the profit on each service. Tahwisa is an internal tool, so it has no public link.

waity.title: Waity
waity.summary: I am building Waity for clinics. Patients check their place in line on a phone, wait nearby, and return when their turn gets close.
waity.contribution: I planned the product, designed the patient and staff screens, and built the first web app.
waity.result: The goal is fewer people in the waiting room, fewer questions at reception, and less time spent managing the line. Waity is still in development.

images.mobileAlt: Waity patient and clinic mobile queue interface

context.title: Patients wait for hours inside the clinic
context.body: The waiting room fills up. Patients get tired, and reception answers the same question all day: when is my turn?

build.title: I put the waiting line on the phone
build.body: Patients see their place, how many people are ahead, and when to return. Staff move the line from one simple screen.

outcome.title: Still in development
outcome.body: The goal is a calmer waiting room and less work at reception. We need real clinic use before we measure the result.

awid.title: Awid
awid.summary: I am building Awid for local delivery in Algeria. A customer posts a shopping list, pickup, or package. A nearby driver then offers a price.
awid.contribution: I planned the product, the nearby-driver search, the delivery steps, and the first app.
awid.result: The goal is simple local delivery for customers and more paid work for independent drivers. Awid is coming soon.

images.cardAlt: Awid coming soon and under development
images.mobileAlt: Awid mobile app coming soon and under development
images.desktopAlt: Awid platform coming soon and under development

context.title: Most delivery apps stop at food
context.body: People also need groceries, store pickups, and packages moved across town. Those jobs are often arranged through calls and messages.

build.title: I made the request and price clear
build.body: The customer posts the job. Awid finds nearby drivers. One driver offers a price, and the customer accepts or refuses it.

outcome.title: Coming soon
outcome.body: I am building the first version now. It has no users or launch results yet.

howIWork.title: How I take a project from rough idea to build.
howIWork.body: Discovery, scope, investment, and responsibilities get clear before development starts.

about.title: The person behind the build.

howIWork.title: How I work
howIWork.intro: A useful project starts with the business case: who needs it, what should become easier, where the value is, and what counts as a win.

discovery.label: Discovery call
discovery.value: Project context, target users, current workflow, risks, and success metrics get mapped first.

mvp.label: MVP shape
mvp.value: The first working version is defined clearly. Nice-to-have features wait.

agreement.label: Agreement
agreement.value: Scope, investment, timeline, milestones, and responsibilities are written before build starts.

chat.clientStart: Hey Heithem. I want to launch a store, startup, or web app. What should be clear before we start?
chat.heithemIntro: Happy to help. Send the rough version first: what the product should do, who will use it, and where it should make money or save time.
chat.heithemCall: A free 30-minute voice or video call is usually enough to map the idea, the risks, the first version, and the success metric.
chat.clientInvestment: Good. What kind of investment should I expect for the web app?
chat.heithemInvestment: The investment becomes clear after discovery. It depends on scope, complexity, timeline, integrations, and what the first version needs to prove.
chat.heithemRange: For a working online store with the important parts included, investment usually starts around $1.5k to $3k. Complex platforms need discovery first, then a clean number.
chat.clientCall: Makes sense. Let’s start with the call.
chat.callNote: Discovery call: project goal, users, MVP scope, risks, timeline, and success metrics.
chat.heithemAgreement: Next comes a short agreement: scope, investment, timeline, milestones, what is included, and what is needed from your side.
chat.heithemClose: Perfect. Once you give the OK on the agreement, work starts.

faq.title: What clients ask before we start
faq.intro: These are the questions clients ask me most often.

installation.question: Do you need to visit my business to install the system?
installation.answer: No. We handle the full setup online. Web apps open from a link. For a local desktop system, you install a small launcher and enter the licence key. I send you the admin link and your access tokens.

hosting.question: Where do you deploy the app, and who pays for it?
hosting.answer: You choose any available domain, and I can set it up for you. I suggest hosting based on the number of users and the app’s needs. Free plans include Vercel and Netlify. Paid options include Hostinger, Oracle Cloud, a VPS, or AWS for large company systems. If you already chose a provider, we use it. You pay the domain and hosting fees directly.

price.question: How much does a project cost?
price.answer: The price depends on the work, time, and project size. I price each project after we agree on the scope.

maintenance.question: Do you offer support after launch?
maintenance.answer: Yes. Basic questions and help after handover are free. Ongoing maintenance and technical support are available when needed for a monthly fee.

about.title: Web apps that move the business.

paragraphs.one: Specialized in building web apps using software engineering knowledge, turning complex business problems into clean, functional systems.
paragraphs.two: The work fits stores, startups, dashboards, and platforms where the app needs to handle real logic, not only look good on the first screen.
paragraphs.three: The goal is simple: create a product that helps sell, manage, decide, or save time through something people can use every day.

about.centerBody: Working for 2 startups as their tech co-founder and decision maker on the tech side of the work.

one.title: Experience aimed at business value.
one.text: With 5 years in engineering and 2 years developing web apps for startups and business owners, the focus is on targeted products designed to bring value to the investor based on the project’s real needs.

two.title: The client’s field becomes part of the app.
two.text: The best web apps feel specific. The client’s experience in the field becomes part of the product, then gets shaped into clean UI, strong speed, secure logic, and a web app that brings more value to the table.
